teacherNotes.title: Anticipated Problems & Solutions (CELTA Standard)
teacherNotes.content:
⚠️ Problem: Learner struggles with rare words like "choir" or "quay".
💡 Solution: Classify as top 100 historical irregulars: choir = /ˈkwaɪər/, quay = /kiː/.

elements.content: Gabarit 14 Champs: Complete Grapheme-to-Phoneme Equivalence & Top Exceptions
1. Definition: Comprehensive codification of the 44 phonemes of English mapped against all productive graphemes and high-frequency exceptions.

2. Rule: English is 85% rule-governed through grapheme-phoneme correspondence rules. The remaining 15% consists of ~100 high-frequency irregular words (the, of, have, said, do, come, some, done, two, been, does, colonel, choir, island) requiring direct lexical retrieval.
3. Why? Systematizes the orthographic code while accounting for historical irregularity.
4. How to recognize? Identify regular grapheme patterns vs irregular lexical items.

5. Common examples: colonel /ˈkɜːrnəl/ (French loanword with historical r-sound), choir /ˈkwaɪər/ (Latinate respelling), island /ˈaɪlənd/ (s inserted by false analogy with isle), quay /kiː/, gauge /ɡeɪdʒ/
6. Counter-examples: Standard regular GPC mappings.
7. Exceptions: Top 100 high-frequency irregular sight words.
8. Common mistakes: Trying to decode "colonel" phonetically as *co-lo-nel.
9. Mnemonic / Hint: Master the 85% rules, memorize the 15% exceptions!
10. Key vocabulary: grapheme-to-phoneme correspondence, GPC, orthographic mapping, lexical exception, complete reference
11. Frequency: ★★★★★ (Mastery)
12. CEFR Level: ⚫ C2
13. Associated Visual: 📊 Complete 44-phoneme grid mapped to productive graphemes.
14. Key Takeaway: 85% of English is rule-governed! Master the rules, memorize top exceptions!

teacherNotes.title: Teacher CCQ Script
teacherNotes.content: Ask these concept checking questions to verify rule understanding without translation:

elements.content: Rule Understanding Check (CCQ):
CCQ 1: What percentage of English words follow regular spelling-to-sound rules? (~85%)
CCQ 2: How is the word "colonel" pronounced in English? (/ˈkɜːrnəl/ kernel)
CCQ 3: Why is there a silent "s" in "island"? (Inserted by 16th-century scholars due to false analogy with French "isle")

teacherNotes.title: Stage aim
teacherNotes.content: Auditory discrimination, minimal pairs, and guided oral drill repetition.

elements.content: Identify the correct expert pronunciation for these famous irregular words:
🎯 Item: colonel ➔ Answer / Pronunciation: /ˈkɜːrnəl/ (sounds like kernel)
🎯 Item: choir ➔ Answer / Pronunciation: /ˈkwaɪər/ (sounds like quire)
🎯 Item: island ➔ Answer / Pronunciation: /ˈaɪlənd/ (silent s)
